title: Clickstream analytics
like: the page-view tracking behind a product analytics tool
brief: Every tap and page view on a busy site sends a tiny event to you. Hundreds of millions pile up each day. Analysts open dashboards to ask what happened this hour. Never drop an event, and keep the storage bill under control as the pile grows.

clarify.a: A few minutes behind is fine. Nobody needs the exact second.

clarify.q: Can an event be counted twice?
clarify.a: Rarely and a little is acceptable for page views, but lost events are not.

clarify.q: How long do we keep raw events?
clarify.a: Recent data stays handy for a month. Older data is rarely read and can go to cheap storage.

requirements.users: Events from 30 million visitors a month (approx.)
notes: About 300 million events a day, each about 0.5 KB (approx.).
Roughly 150 GB of new raw data a day (approx.).

numbers.label: Raw data after one year
numbers.how: 150 GB × 365 ≈ 55 TB (approx.). Cold storage costs about a fifth of hot storage.

hints: Events arrive far faster than people read dashboards. What can sit between the two?
An event stream takes the flood, a stream processor rolls it up into small summaries, and old raw data moves to cheap storage.
Load balancer, collectors, event stream, stream processor, a data lake for raw events, a warehouse that answers the dashboards, and a cold archive.

editorial.summary: Write once into a durable stream, then split the work. A processor turns the flood into small summaries that dashboards read quickly, while raw events settle in a data lake and move to cold storage as they age.

designs.name: Stream in, summaries out, tiered storage
designs.why: The stream absorbs bursts without dropping events. Summaries keep dashboards fast and cheap. The lake keeps raw events for deep questions and a cold archive takes the old ones at a fraction of the price.

tradeoffs: Dashboards a few minutes behind are far cheaper than live ones, because summaries are built in batches.
Keeping raw events lets analysts ask new questions later, but storage grows every day. Tiering keeps it affordable.
Sampling events cuts cost sharply, but a rare event may vanish from the numbers.
A stream with several days of retention lets you replay after a bug, at the price of extra storage.
editorial.realWorld: Busy products collect hundreds of millions to billions of events a day. Teams keep a few weeks hot, summarise the rest, and move raw history to storage that costs a few cents per GB-month (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Clickstream analytics: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A durable copy across the required failure boundary before acknowledgement
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
